source_text: Ἕτεροι δὲ εἰς τὰ ἐναντία περιάγονται πάθη. Δυσέλπιδές εἰσι, καὶ κατηφεῖς, καὶ ὀδυνηροὶ, καὶ δακρυώδεις, καὶ ψοφοδεεῖς, καὶ εὐπτόητοι. Ὁ αὐτὸς οἶνος ἐν διαφόροις σωμάτων ἕξεσι διάφορα τὰ πάθη ταῖς ψυχαῖς ἐργαζόμενος. Οἷς μὲν γὰρ ἂν διάχυσιν τοῦ αἵματος ἐμποιήσας πρὸς τὴν ἐπιφάνειαν ἐξανθήσῃ, φαιδροὺς καὶ ἡδεῖς καὶ γεγανωμένους αὐτοὺς ἀποδείκνυσιν· ὧν δ' ἂν ὑπὸ τοῦ βάρους καταπιλήσῃ τὴν ἕξιν, συστέλλων αὐτῶν καὶ καταπιέζων τὸ αἷμα, πρὸς τὴν ἐναντίαν αὐτοὺς περιάγει διάθεσιν. Καὶ τί δεῖ λέγειν τῶν λοιπῶν παθῶν τὸν ὄχλον; τὰς δυσκολίας τοῦ ἤθους; τὸ εὐπαρόξυντον; τὸ μεμψίμοιρον; τὸ ὀξύῤῥοπον τῆς ψυχῆς; τὴν κραυγήν; τὸν θόρυβον; τὸ πρὸς πᾶσαν ἀπάτην εὐπαράγωγον; τὸ πρὸς τὰς ὀργὰς ἀταμίευτον; Ἡ δὲ πρὸς τὰς ἡδονὰς ἀκρασία ἄντικρυς ὥσπερ ἐκ πηγῆς τοῦ οἴνου φέρεται, καὶ συνεισπίπτει τῷ ἀκράτῳ τῆς ἀσελγείας ἡ νόσος, πᾶσαν βοσκημάτων μανίαν ἐπὶ τὸ θῆλυ δευτέραν τῆς τῶν μεθυόντων ὕβρεως ἀποφαίνουσα· εἴπερ τὰ μὲν ἄλογα γνωρίζει τοὺς ὅρους τῆς φύσεως, οἱ δὲ μεθύοντες ἐν ἄῤῥενι μὲν τὸ θῆλυ, ἐν δὲ τῷ θήλει τὸ ἄῤῥεν ἐπιζητοῦσιν. Οὐδὲ ἐπεξελθεῖν τῷ λόγῳ ῥᾴδιον πᾶσι τοῖς ἐκ τῆς μέθης δεινοῖς. Αἱ μὲν οὖν ἐκ τοῦ λοιμοῦ βλάβαι χρόνῳ ἐγγίνονται τοῖς ἀνθρώποις, κατὰ μικρὸν τοῦ ἀέρος τὴν παρ' ἑαυτοῦ φθορὰν ἐντιθέντος τοῖς σώμασιν· αἱ δὲ παρὰ τοῦ οἴνου εὐθὺς συνεισπίπτουσιν. Οὕτω γὰρ τὴν ψυχὴν ἀπολωλότες, ὡς ὑπὸ πάσης κηλῖδος εἶναι κατεστιγμένοι, ἔτι καὶ αὐτὴν τοῦ σώ ματος τὴν ἕξιν προσδιαφθείρονται· οὐ μόνον τῇ ὑπερβολῇ τῶν ἡδονῶν ἐξοιστρουσῶν ἐπὶ λαγνείας ἐκτετηκότες καὶ διαῤῥέοντες, ἀλλὰ καὶ αὐτῷ τῷ ὄγκῳ πεπλαδηκὸς καὶ βρυῶδες καὶ τοῦ ζωτικοῦ τόνου λελυμένον τὸ σῶμα φέροντες. Τούτων πελιδνοὶ οἱ ὀφθαλμοί· ὕπωχρος δὲ ἡ ἐπιφάνεια· πνεῦμα προσ εστηκός· γλῶσσα παρειμένη, καὶ κραυγὴ ἄση μος· ἀκροσφαλεῖς οἱ πόδες καθάπερ οἱ τῶν παίδων· ἐκκρίσεις δὲ τῶν περιττωμάτων αὐτόματοι ὥσπερ ἀπὸ ἀψύχων ῥέουσαι. Ἐλεεινοὶ τῆς τρυφῆς, ἐλεεινό τεροι τῶν ἐν πελάγει χειμαζομένων, οὓς ἄλλα ἐξ ἄλ λων διαδεχόμενα καὶ ἐπιβαπτίζοντα κύματα ἀναφέ ρειν οὐκ ἐπιτρέπει τοῦ κλύδωνος. Οὕτω δὴ καὶ τού των αἱ ψυχαὶ ὑποβρύχιοι φέρονται βεβαπτισμέναι τῷ οἴνῳ. Διόπερ ὡς τὰ χειμαζόμενα πλοῖα, ἐπειδὰν ὑπέραντλα γένηται, ἀναγκαίως τῇ ἐκβολῇ τοῦ φόρτου κουφίζεται· οὕτω καὶ τούτοις ἀναγκαῖαι τῶν βαρυνόντων αἱ ἀποθέσεις. Ἐμοῦντες γὰρ καὶ ἀποβλύ ζοντες, μόλις ἐλευθεροῦνται τοῦ βάρους· τοσοῦτον τῶν δυσπλοούντων ἐλεεινότεροι, ὅσον οἱ μὲν ἀνέμους καὶ θάλασσαν καὶ τὰς ἔξωθεν ἀνάγκας ἐπαιτιῶνται· οἱ δὲ αὐθαίρετον ἐπισπῶνται τὸν ἐκ τῆς μέθης χει μῶνα. Ὁ δαιμονῶν ἐλεεινός· ὁ δὲ μεθύων, τὰ αὐτὰ πάσχων, οὐδὲ τοῦ ἐλεεῖσθαι ἄξιος, αὐθαιρέτῳ δαίμονι προσπαλαίων. Οἳ καὶ μέθης συντιθέασι φάρμακα, οὐχὶ τὸ μὴ παθεῖν τι δεινὸν ἀπὸ τοῦ οἴνου, ἀλλὰ τὸ μὴ διαλείπειν μεθύοντες μηχανώμενοι. Ὀλίγη μὲν γὰρ αὐτοῖς ἡ ἡμέρα· μικρὰ δὲ ἡ νὺξ καὶ ἡ χειμέριος, πρός γε τὸν τοῦ πότου χρόνον. Τέλος δὲ οὐκ ἔστι τοῦ κακοῦ. Αὐτὸς γὰρ ἑαυτὸν ὁ οἶνος ἐπὶ τὸ πλεῖον προάγει. Οὐ γὰρ τὴν χρείαν παραμυθεῖται, ἀλλ' ἑτέρου πότου χρείαν ἀπαραίτητον ἐμποιεῖ, ἐκκαίων τοὺς μεθύοντας, καὶ ἀεὶ πρὸς τὴν τοῦ πλείο νος ἔφεσιν προκαλούμενος.
orientation: Basil continues his description of drunkards, now contrasting the opposite emotional states wine produces and arguing that drunkenness is a self-inflicted storm worse than demon possession.
pass_a_gloss: But others are led around into the opposite passions. They are despairing, and downcast, and full of pain, and tearful, and fearful of noise, and easily terrified. The same wine, in different conditions of bodies, produces different passions in the souls. For in those in whom, having produced a diffusion of the blood, it blooms out to the surface, it shows them bright and pleasant and beaming; but in those whose condition it has pressed down by its weight, contracting and squeezing their blood, it leads them around into the opposite disposition. And why is it necessary to speak of the crowd of the remaining passions? the difficulties of character? the quickness to anger? the fault-finding? the instability of the soul? the shouting? the uproar? the being easily led astray toward every deceit? the being unrestrained toward fits of anger? But the lack of self-control toward pleasures plainly, as from a spring, is borne from the wine, and the disease rushes in together with the unmixed wantonness, showing every frenzy of grazing animals toward the female to be second to the outrage of drunkards; since indeed the irrational animals know the boundaries of nature, but the drunkards seek the female in the male, and the male in the female. Nor is it easy to go through in speech all the terrible things from drunkenness. The harms from plague, then, come to humans in time, as the air little by little puts its corruption into the bodies; but the harms from wine rush in immediately. For having lost the soul in this way, so as to be marked by every stain, they still further ruin the very condition of the body; not only worn out and dissolved by the excess of pleasures goading them toward lusts, but also carrying the body swollen and sodden with the very bulk and loosened from the vital tone. Of these the eyes are livid; the surface is pale; the breath is foul; the tongue is slack, and the cry is inarticulate; the feet are unsteady like those of children; and the discharges of the excesses flow out automatically as from lifeless things. Pitiable in their luxury, more pitiable than those storm-tossed on the sea, whom waves succeeding one another and overwhelming do not permit to rise up from the swell. So indeed the souls of these are carried under water, baptized in wine. Therefore, as storm-tossed ships, whenever they become waterlogged, are necessarily lightened by the throwing out of the cargo; so also for these the removal of the things weighing them down is necessary. For vomiting and spitting out, they are barely freed from the weight; so much more pitiable than those who sail badly, as the latter blame winds and sea and external necessities; but the former draw upon themselves the self-chosen storm from drunkenness. The demon-possessed person is pitiable; but the drunkard, suffering the same things, is not even worthy of pity, wrestling with a self-chosen demon. They also compound drugs of drunkenness, contriving not to suffer something terrible from the wine, but not to stop being drunkards. For the day is short for them; and the night is small, even the wintry one, at least for the time of drinking. And there is no end of the evil. For wine itself leads itself on to more. For it does not comfort the need, but produces an unavoidable need of another drink, inflaming the drunkards, and always summoning them toward the desire for more.

choices.term: Ἕτεροι δὲ εἰς τὰ ἐναντία περιάγονται πάθη
choices.english: But others are led around into the opposite passions
choices.why: περιάγονται is passive, suggesting wine as the agent leading them around; 'passions' preserves πάθη as emotional states rather than 'sufferings'
rejected: But others are carried into opposite sufferings
But others turn to opposite emotions

choices.term: Ὁ αὐτὸς οἶνος ἐν διαφόροις σωμάτων ἕξεσι διάφορα τὰ πάθη ταῖς ψυχαῖς ἐργαζόμενος
choices.english: The same wine, in different conditions of bodies, produces different passions in the souls
choices.why: ἕξεσι means bodily conditions or states, not 'temperaments'; the participle ἐργαζόμενος is causal, explaining why the same wine has opposite effects
rejected: The same wine working different passions in souls according to different bodily states
One wine produces different emotions in different bodily constitutions

choices.term: ἡ δὲ πρὸς τὰς ἡδονὰς ἀκρασία
choices.english: the lack of self-control toward pleasures
choices.why: ἀκρασία is lack of self-control or incontinence, distinct from ἀσέλγεια (wantonness) which follows; keeping them separate avoids conflation

choices.term: συνεισπίπτει τῷ ἀκράτῳ τῆς ἀσελγείας ἡ νόσος
choices.english: the disease rushes in together with the unmixed wantonness
choices.why: ἀκράτῳ here means 'unmixed' or 'pure', playing on the wine imagery; ἀσέλγεια is wantonness or licentiousness, distinct from ἀκρασία
rejected: the disease of wantonness rushes in together with the unrestraint
the sickness falls in with the unmixed licentiousness

choices.term: πᾶσαν βοσκημάτων μανίαν ἐπὶ τὸ θῆλυ δευτέραν τῆς τῶν μεθυόντων ὕβρεως ἀποφαίνουσα
choices.english: showing every frenzy of grazing animals toward the female to be second to the outrage of drunkards
choices.why: δευτέραν means 'second to' i.e. inferior; the animal frenzy is the thing shown as second, and the drunkards' outrage is the standard of comparison
rejected: making the frenzy of grazing animals toward the female second to the outrage of drunkards
declaring every animal madness toward the female inferior to the drunkards' outrage

choices.term: Αὐτὸς γὰρ ἑαυτὸν ὁ οἶνος ἐπὶ τὸ πλεῖον προάγει
choices.english: For wine itself leads itself on to more
choices.why: The reflexive ἑαυτόν is emphatic: wine is personified as self-propagating, leading itself on, not leading a person
rejected: For wine itself leads a person on to more
For wine itself advances itself to more

pass_b_english: Others are led around into the opposite passions. They are despairing, downcast, full of pain and tears, fearful of every noise, easily terrified. The same wine, in different conditions of bodies, produces different passions in the souls. For when it makes the blood diffuse and bloom out toward the surface, it renders people bright, pleasant, and cheerful. But when it presses down the body's condition by its weight, constricting and crushing the blood, it leads them around into the opposite disposition. And why should I speak of the crowd of remaining passions? The difficulty of their character, their quickness to anger, their fault-finding, the instability of their soul, the shouting, the uproar, their easy seduction into every deceit, their unrestrained rage? The lack of self-control toward pleasures flows straight out as from a spring of wine, and the disease rushes in together with the unmixed wantonness, showing every frenzy of grazing animals toward the female to be second to the outrage of drunkards. For the irrational animals know the boundaries of nature, but drunkards seek the female in the male and the male in the female. It is not easy to go through in speech all the evils that come from drunkenness. The harms from a plague come upon people over time, as the air gradually introduces its corruption into their bodies; but the harms from wine rush in immediately. For having lost their souls in this way, so as to be marked with every stain, they further corrupt the very condition of their body. They are not only worn out and dissipated by the excess of pleasures that goad them toward lust, but they also carry a body made flabby and bloated by its very bulk, with its vital tone dissolved. Their eyes are livid, their surface is pale, their breath is labored, their tongue is slack, and their cry is inarticulate. Their feet totter like those of children, and their excretions flow out on their own as from lifeless bodies. Pitiable in their luxury, they are more pitiable than those storm-tossed at sea, whom wave after wave, overtaking and submerging them, does not allow to rise from the swell. So too the souls of these people are carried beneath the surface, sunk in wine. Therefore, just as storm-tossed ships, when they become waterlogged, are necessarily lightened by throwing out the cargo, so for these people the removal of what weighs them down is necessary. For by vomiting and spewing forth, they are barely freed from the weight. They are so much more pitiable than those who sail badly, in that the latter blame the winds and the sea and external necessities, while the former draw upon themselves a self-chosen storm from drunkenness. The demon-possessed person is pitiable; but the drunkard, suffering the same things, is not even worthy of pity, since he wrestles with a self-chosen demon. They even compound drugs for drunkenness, not to avoid suffering something terrible from wine, but to contrive not to stop being drunk. For the day is short for them, and the night is short, even the winter night, compared to the time of drinking. And there is no end to the evil. For wine itself leads itself on to more. It does not relieve the need, but creates an unavoidable need for another drink, inflaming the drunkards and always summoning them toward the desire for more.

problems.why: προσεστηκός means 'standing by/attending' or 'labored breathing,' not 'foul.' The breath is obstructed or heavy, not malodorous.
ἀποβλύζω means 'gushing out' or 'spewing forth,' describing involuntary vomiting, not active 'rinsing out.'
problems.ruling: ἀποβλύζοντες means 'gushing/spewing forth,' not 'rinsing out.' Misleads reader about involuntary vomiting vs. active rinsing.

fixed: πνεῦμα προσεστηκός means 'breath standing by/attending' or 'labored breathing,' not 'foul'; changed to 'labored.'
ἀποβλύζοντες means 'gushing out' or 'spewing forth,' not active 'rinsing out'; changed to 'spewing forth.'

last_rejected.quote: their easy seduction into every deceit
last_rejected.why: ἀπάτη here means 'error' or 'delusion' (mental deception), not 'deceit' (intentional trickery by others).
last_rejected.fix: their easy lapse into every delusion
last_rejected.ruling: ἀπάτη covers both 'deceit' and 'delusion'; 'deceit' is within normal range, not a major error.

last_rejected.why: ἀκράτῳ is 'unmixed' (of wine), but here it describes ἀσελγείας; 'unmixed wantonness' is awkward. Better: 'the unmixed wine of wantonness' or 'undiluted wantonness'.
last_rejected.ruling: ἀκράτῳ can mean 'undiluted' metaphorically; 'unmixed wantonness' is awkward but not a meaning change.
